rows.question: How long will you pay for a hotel if my house is unlivable after a fire?
rows.answer:
**If the fire is a covered loss that makes your home unfit to live in, the policy pays additional living expenses, such as a hotel, for the shortest time needed to repair or replace the damage, up to a maximum of 12 months.**

**What's covered:** If a loss covered under this Section makes the residence premises not fit to live in, we cover Additional Living Expense: any necessary increase in living expenses incurred by you so that your household can maintain its normal standard of living. This covers the *extra* cost of living elsewhere, beyond your normal expenses, while your home can't be lived in.

**How long:** Payment will be for the shortest time required to repair or replace the damage or, if you permanently relocate, the shortest time for your household to settle elsewhere, but not to exceed 12 months.

**Dollar cap:** The limit for Coverage D is 30% of the Coverage A limit. Coverage A is the dwelling limit shown on your Declarations page. For example, if your dwelling limit were $300,000, the cap for living expenses would be $90,000. Check your Declarations page for your actual figure.

**If the fire was next door instead:** If your home isn't damaged but officials bar you from it because of the fire, if a civil authority prohibits you from using the residence premises because of direct damage to neighboring premises by a covered peril, we cover Additional Living Expense for no more than two weeks.

**Things that could affect your claim:**
- Coverage applies only if the fire is a covered loss. We do not cover any loss arising out of any act an insured commits with the intent to cause a loss.
- You're also expected to protect your property after the fire. We do not cover loss caused by neglect, meaning failure of an insured to use all reasonable means to save and preserve property at and after the time of a loss.

This explains what the policy language says. The final decision on your claim will be made by your adjuster. Keep your hotel receipts and other records of extra expenses to support it.

rows.question: How long will you pay for a hotel if a wildfire destroys my house?
rows.answer:
**It depends mainly on whether the Governor declared a state of emergency for the wildfire.** Without a declaration, the standard limit is 12 months. With one, your California endorsement extends this to up to 24 months, and possibly up to 36 months. Either way, the fire damage must be a covered loss under your policy.

**What pays for the hotel**
Hotel and other extra living costs fall under Additional Living Expense (Coverage D). If a covered loss makes your home unfit to live in, the policy covers any necessary increase in living expenses incurred by you so that your household can maintain its normal standard of living.

**How long, under the standard policy**
Payment will be for the shortest time required to repair or replace the damage or, if you permanently relocate, the shortest time for your household to settle elsewhere, but not to exceed 12 months.

**How long in California, if a state of emergency is declared**
The California endorsement changes the standard rule. If a covered loss relates to a state of emergency declared by the Governor, Additional Living Expense is payable for a period of up to 24 months instead of 12 months. In addition, we will grant an extension of up to 12 additional months, for a total of 36 months, if you act in good faith and with reasonable diligence and encounter delays in reconstruction beyond your control.

**Getting money up front**
If a covered loss relating to a declared state of emergency makes the residence premises uninhabitable, we will provide an advance payment of no less than four months of Additional Living Expense upon request. You have to ask for this advance.

**Dollar limit**
There is also a cap on the total amount, separate from the time limit. The limit for Coverage D is 30% of the Coverage A limit. Your Coverage A (dwelling) limit is shown on your Declarations page.

**If authorities block access but your house isn't damaged**
If the fire damages nearby properties rather than your home, and officials bar you from your home because of that damage, a shorter limit applies. Under the standard policy, if this happens because of direct damage to neighboring premises by a covered peril, we cover Additional Living Expense for no more than two weeks. In California, the two-week civil authority limit in HO-3 Section 2.5 is replaced with a limit of four weeks for California residence premises.

This explains what the policy language says. Whether your claim is covered and how much is paid will be decided by the claims process based on your specific facts.

unsupported_claims: Your Coverage A (dwelling) limit is shown on your Declarations page.

rows.question: Can I get an advance on living expenses after a wildfire?
rows.answer:
**Yes, possibly. In California, you can request an advance of at least four months of living expenses, but only if the wildfire damage is a covered loss related to a declared state of emergency and it makes your home unlivable.** The endorsement says that if a covered loss relating to a declared state of emergency makes the residence premises uninhabitable, we will provide an advance payment of no less than four months of Additional Living Expense upon request.

**What this depends on:**
- **Whether a state of emergency was declared** for the wildfire. If none was declared, this advance provision doesn't apply.
- **Whether the damage is a covered loss** under your policy.
- **Whether your home is uninhabitable.**
- **Whether you ask for it.** The advance is paid "upon request," so contact your adjuster.

**How long living expenses can last:**
- **Standard policy:** Under the base HO-3 form, payment will be for the shortest time required to repair or replace the damage or, if you permanently relocate, the shortest time for your household to settle elsewhere, but not to exceed 12 months.
- **California extension:** In California, the endorsement extends this period, but only for emergencies declared by the Governor. If a covered loss relates to a state of emergency declared by the Governor, Additional Living Expense is payable for a period of up to 24 months instead of 12 months.
- **Further extension:** In the same Governor-declared emergency situation, we will grant an extension of up to 12 additional months, for a total of 36 months, if you act in good faith and with reasonable diligence and encounter delays in reconstruction beyond your control.
- **Dollar cap:** The limit for Coverage D is 30% of the Coverage A limit. Your exact amount depends on the Coverage A limit on your Declarations page.

**Related help if your home was a total loss:**
- **Advance for your belongings:** If the total loss relates to a declared state of emergency, we will offer a payment under Coverage C of no less than 30% of the Coverage C limit, up to $250,000, without requiring an itemized inventory.
- **More time to claim replacement cost:** For a total loss relating to a declared state of emergency, the 180-day period in HO-3 Section 6.3 to make a claim for additional replacement cost is replaced with a period of no less than 36 months from the date of the first actual cash value payment.

**If authorities order you out:** If a civil authority bars you from your home because a covered peril damaged neighboring property, the California endorsement extends living expense coverage. The two-week civil authority limit in HO-3 Section 2.5 is replaced with a limit of four weeks for California residence premises.

This explains what the policy language says and isn't a coverage decision or a promise of payment. Your adjuster will confirm whether your loss qualifies.

rows.question: What's my deductible for hail damage?
rows.answer:
**Your hail deductible is a percentage of your dwelling (Coverage A) limit: 1%, 2%, or 5%, whichever is shown on your Declarations page. It is never less than $1,000.** I can't tell you the exact dollar amount without your Coverage A limit and the percentage on your Declarations page.

**How it works in Texas**

Your Texas endorsement replaces the standard deductible for wind and hail losses. For loss caused by windstorm or hail, the deductible in HO-3 Section 6.1 is replaced by a deductible equal to the percentage of the Coverage A limit shown in the Declarations for this endorsement. The available percentages are 1%, 2%, and 5%. The windstorm or hail deductible will not be less than $1,000.

**Example from the policy:** If the Coverage A limit is $300,000 and the Declarations show a 2% windstorm or hail deductible, the deductible for a hail loss is $6,000. We will pay only that part of the loss that exceeds $6,000.

**Other details**

- **One deductible per storm, for all coverages together:** The windstorm or hail deductible applies to the total of all loss payable under Coverages A, B and C combined that results from a single windstorm or hail event. This means you pay one deductible across your home, other structures, and belongings, not one for each. Also, all windstorm or hail damage occurring within any 72-hour period is considered a single event.
- **Cosmetic roof damage isn't covered:** We do not cover cosmetic damage to roof surfacing caused by hail. This means dents or pitting that only change how the roof looks. It does not apply if the damage stops the roof from keeping water out or shortens its expected life.
- **Report the claim within one year:** A claim for windstorm or hail damage must be reported to us within one year after the date of the windstorm or hail event, unless good cause exists for later reporting.

Whether a specific loss is covered, and how much is paid, will be decided when the claim is reviewed.

rows.question: If my dwelling limit is $300,000 and I have a 2% wind deductible, how much is my deductible?
rows.answer:
**Your windstorm or hail deductible would be $6,000** (2% of your $300,000 dwelling limit). This deductible applies only to damage caused by windstorm or hail.

**How it works**
- In Texas, for loss caused by windstorm or hail, the deductible in HO-3 Section 6.1 is replaced by a deductible equal to the percentage of the Coverage A limit shown in the Declarations for this endorsement. Coverage A is your dwelling coverage.
- The policy gives this exact example: If the Coverage A limit is $300,000 and the Declarations show a 2% windstorm or hail deductible, the deductible for a hail loss is $6,000. We will pay only that part of the loss that exceeds $6,000.
- The available percentages are 1%, 2%, and 5%. The windstorm or hail deductible will not be less than $1,000.

**Things to keep in mind**
- Check your Declarations page to confirm the percentage. The 2% applies only if that is what your Declarations show for this endorsement.
- For damage that isn't caused by windstorm or hail, your regular policy deductible applies instead. That amount isn't in the documents I have.
- For a hail claim on your roof, we do not cover cosmetic damage to roof surfacing caused by hail. That means dents or marks that change how the roof looks but don't stop it from keeping water out or shorten its life.

This explains what the policy language says. Whether a particular claim is covered depends on the facts of the loss.

rows.question: Hail dented my roof but it doesn't leak. Is that covered?
rows.answer:
**Probably not, if the dents are only cosmetic. But it depends on whether the hail shortened your roof's expected life, not just on whether it leaks.** Under the Texas Windstorm and Hail Deductible Endorsement, we do not cover cosmetic damage to roof surfacing caused by hail.

**What counts as "cosmetic"**

The endorsement defines cosmetic damage as marring, pitting or denting that changes the appearance of the roof surface but does not prevent the roof from continuing to function as a barrier to water entering the dwelling, and does not shorten the expected life of the roof.

A roof that doesn't leak meets only part of that definition. If the dents shorten the roof's expected life, the damage would not fall under this exclusion. An adjuster's inspection would determine that, and I can't make that determination from here.

**If the damage turns out not to be cosmetic**, a few other provisions would affect what's paid:

- **Roof age:** Loss to roof surfacing caused by windstorm or hail is settled at actual cash value, not replacement cost, if the roof surfacing is more than 15 years old at the time of loss. Actual cash value accounts for depreciation, so it's typically less than the cost of a new roof. Roof surfacing 15 years old or less is settled under HO-3 Section 6.3.
- **Deductible:** Your hail deductible is a percentage of your dwelling coverage, as shown on your Declarations page. For example, if the Coverage A limit is $300,000 and the Declarations show a 2% windstorm or hail deductible, the deductible for a hail loss is $6,000. We will pay only that part of the loss that exceeds $6,000. Check your Declarations for your actual percentage and limit.
- **One storm, one deductible:** All windstorm or hail damage occurring within any 72-hour period is considered a single event, and the deductible applies to the combined loss across your dwelling, other structures, and personal property.

**If your roof develops damage that needs protecting**, the policy will pay the reasonable cost incurred by you for necessary measures taken solely to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage, such as tarping a damaged roof. Keep your receipts.

This explains the policy language only. The final coverage decision would come from the claims process after an inspection.

rows.question: Is flood damage covered by my homeowners policy?
rows.answer:
**No. Your homeowners policy (HO-3) does not cover flood damage.** The policy excludes it, and flood coverage is available only through a separate flood policy.

**What the exclusion covers**

The HO-3 says we do not cover loss caused by: flood, surface water, waves, tidal water, or overflow of a body of water, whether or not driven by wind. This applies even if wind pushed the water into your home, such as during a storm.

The same section also excludes two other kinds of water damage that people often think of as flooding:
- Water or water-borne material that backs up through sewers or drains or overflows from a sump pump. However, water backup coverage is available by endorsement with a sublimit. That means you could have this coverage only if you added that endorsement, and it pays only up to a capped amount. Check your Declarations page to see whether you have it.
- Water below the surface of the ground that seeps through a foundation, basement floor or wall.

**Related benefits**

Benefits like debris removal and additional living expenses usually won't apply to flood damage, because they depend on the loss being covered:
- Debris removal is paid if a covered peril causes the loss.
- Additional Living Expense applies if a loss covered under this Section makes the residence premises not fit to live in.

**If your car is damaged by flood**

Vehicles fall under a separate auto policy. In the Personal Auto Policy, hail, water or flood is listed among losses considered other than collision (comprehensive). Whether your car would be covered depends on whether you have comprehensive coverage on your auto policy.

If you're worried about flooding at your home, consider asking your agent about a separate flood policy and the water backup endorsement. This is a summary of the policy language, not a final coverage decision on any specific claim.

rows.question: Does my homeowners policy cover earthquakes?
rows.answer:
**No. Your standard homeowners policy (HO-3) does not cover earthquake damage, but it does cover fire or explosion caused by an earthquake, and you can buy earthquake coverage separately.**

**What's excluded:** The policy states that we do not cover loss caused by earth movement, including earthquake, landslide, mudflow, sinkhole, or subsidence, regardless of any other cause contributing to the loss. If an earthquake cracks your foundation or damages your walls, the base policy won't pay for that damage.

**The exception for fire and explosion:** However, we do cover direct loss by fire or explosion that results from earth movement. For example, if an earthquake breaks a gas line and your home catches fire, the fire damage would be covered, but not the shaking damage itself.

**Buying earthquake coverage:** Earthquake coverage may be purchased separately by endorsement. Whether you're covered depends on whether you added this endorsement to your policy. I can't see your policy details, so check your Declarations page or contact your agent to find out.

**If fire or explosion follows an earthquake:** The policy will pay the reasonable cost incurred by you for necessary measures taken solely to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage, such as tarping a damaged roof or boarding broken windows. This applies only to damage from a covered peril, such as that fire or explosion, and not to earthquake damage unless you have the endorsement. Keep receipts for these expenses.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a final decision on any specific claim.

rows.question: Is mold covered?
rows.answer:
**Mold is covered only in limited cases: up to $10,000 total, and only when the mold results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst.** If the mold came from something that isn't a covered peril, this coverage wouldn't apply.

**What the policy says:**
- We will pay up to $10,000 in total for direct physical loss caused by fungi, mold, wet or dry rot, or bacteria, including the cost to remove it and to tear out and replace covered property to gain access, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst.
- The $10,000 is a total cap. This is the most we will pay regardless of the number of locations or claims during the policy period. [Applies only when the mold or rot results from a covered peril.]

**What it depends on:**
Whether your mold is covered depends mainly on **what caused it**. A sudden, accidental event like a burst pipe is the kind of cause the policy describes. The cause of your mold isn't clear from your question, so I can't say whether it would qualify.

**A related point that may help:**
If your property is damaged by a covered peril, the policy also helps with steps to prevent more damage. We will pay the reasonable cost incurred by you for necessary measures taken solely to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage, such as tarping a damaged roof or boarding broken windows. Keep receipts for these expenses. For example, if a pipe bursts, quick action to stop the water may help prevent mold. Those costs are covered only when the original damage came from a covered peril.

This explains the policy language and is not a final coverage decision. If you have a mold problem, contact us to report it, and an adjuster will review the cause and the details of your claim.

rows.question: My jewelry was stolen. How much will you pay?
rows.answer:
Under the standard homeowners policy (HO-3), stolen jewelry is subject to a special limit of **$1,500 per loss**, unless you've added higher coverage by endorsement. The policy has a special limit of $1,500 for loss by theft of jewelry, watches, furs, and precious and semiprecious stones.

**What this means for you:**
- **The $1,500 is a total for the whole theft, not per item.** These limits apply to each loss for all property in each category. If several pieces were stolen in the same theft, $1,500 is the most the policy pays for all of them together, along with any watches, furs, or loose stones taken in that theft.
- **You may have higher coverage if you scheduled your jewelry.** Higher limits for scheduled items are available by endorsement. If you added an endorsement listing specific pieces, that endorsement's limits would matter instead. Check your Declarations page or ask your agent whether you have one.

**What I can't tell you from the documents available:**
- Whether you have a scheduled-items endorsement, or what its limits are.
- Your deductible, or how the value of your jewelry will be determined.

This is what the policy language says, not a final decision on your claim. The adjuster handling your claim will determine the actual amount paid.

rows.question: How much cash is covered if it's destroyed in a fire?
rows.answer:
**Your policy pays up to $200 for cash, no matter how much was destroyed.** The HO-3 policy sets $200 on money, bank notes, gold other than goldware, and coins.

**How the limit works:**
- It is a per-loss cap for the whole category. The following special limits apply to each loss for all property in each category. That means $200 is the most for all cash, coins, and similar items combined in a single fire, not $200 per bill or per location.
- Unlike some other categories in this section, such as jewelry or firearms, which are capped only for loss by theft, the cash limit isn't tied to a particular cause. So the $200 cap applies to a fire loss too.
- Cash falls under your personal property coverage (Coverage C), which covers personal property owned or used by an insured while it is anywhere in the world. The $200 special limit sits within your overall Coverage C limit.

**Higher limits:** The policy says that higher limits for scheduled items are available by endorsement. The documents I have don't say whether cash can be scheduled this way. Your agent can tell you what options exist.

**What I can't tell from these documents:** Your deductible, and whether anything else on your Declarations page or in other endorsements changes this. I'm explaining what the policy language says, not deciding your claim. Any payment depends on how your claim is reviewed.

rows.question: A windstorm knocked a tree onto my house. Will you pay to remove it?
rows.answer:
**Yes, your policy includes coverage for removing a tree knocked down by windstorm, as long as the tree damages a covered structure (such as your house) or blocks a driveway.** The amount is capped, and a deductible applies.

**Tree removal**
- We will also pay up to $1,000 in total for the removal of trees felled by windstorm, hail or weight of ice, snow or sleet, with no more than $500 for any one tree, if the tree damages a covered structure or blocks a driveway. For a single tree that fell on your house, that means up to $500 for its removal.

**Your deductible**
- We will pay only that part of the total of all loss payable that exceeds the deductible amount shown in the Declarations. A separate windstorm or hail deductible may apply if shown by endorsement. Check your Declarations page to see which deductible applies to your claim.

**Replacing the tree itself is not covered**
- The policy does pay for trees and plants damaged by certain causes, but we do not cover loss caused by windstorm to trees, shrubs or plants. Removing the fallen tree may be covered, but replacing it with a new one would not be.

**Debris from the damage to your house**
- We will pay your reasonable expense for the removal of debris of covered property if a covered peril causes the loss. This expense is included in the limit of liability that applies to the damaged property. Whether this applies to debris like broken roofing depends on whether the damage to your home is a covered loss. The documents I have don't confirm that, so your adjuster will need to review it.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a final decision on your claim. Your adjuster will make that determination based on the facts and your Declarations page.

rows.question: A pipe has been slowly leaking under my sink for a month. Am I covered?
rows.answer:
**A slow leak lasting a month most likely falls under a listed exclusion for damage to your home, though the final decision depends on the facts and the claim review.** Among the losses your HO-3 policy does not cover is continuous or repeated seepage or leakage of water or steam over a period of 14 or more days from within a plumbing, heating or air conditioning system or household appliance. A leak that has gone on for about a month is well past that 14-day mark.

**What could still matter**

- **Resulting water damage:** The policy says that if any of these cause water damage not otherwise excluded, we cover the resulting water damage, including the cost of tearing out and replacing part of the building to access the system, but not the system or appliance itself. Whether that applies depends on whether the damage counts as "not otherwise excluded." Long-term seepage is itself on the excluded list, so this would need to be reviewed on your specific claim.
- **The pipe itself:** Even where resulting water damage is covered, the policy does not pay for the leaking pipe or plumbing system itself.
- **Mold or rot:** The policy pays up to $10,000 in total for direct physical loss caused by fungi, mold, wet or dry rot, or bacteria, including the cost to remove it and to tear out and replace covered property to gain access, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst. A slow leak excluded under the 14-day rule would generally not meet that condition.
- **Your belongings (cabinet contents, etc.):** Personal property is covered only for specific named perils, which include accidental discharge or overflow of water or steam. The sections I have don't say whether the 14-day seepage rule also applies to belongings, so I can't tell you how a long-term leak would be treated for your personal items.

**Bottom line:** Damage from a leak that has continued for 14 days or more is listed as not covered for your home's structure. Some exceptions could still apply depending on how the damage happened. This isn't a coverage decision. An adjuster would need to review the cause and extent of the damage. In the meantime, it's a good idea to stop the leak and take photos of the damage.

rows.question: How long do I have to send a proof of loss?
rows.answer:
**Under the homeowners policy (HO-3), you have 60 days from when Cobalt Harbor Mutual asks for it.** The policy says you must send to us, within 60 days after our request, your signed, sworn proof of loss.

**What this means:**
- **The 60 days starts when we request the proof of loss**, not on the date of the loss.
- **The proof of loss must be signed and sworn**, meaning it's a formal statement you sign under oath.

**Other duties after a loss:** The proof of loss is one of several things the policy asks you to do. These include:
- Give prompt notice to us or our agent.
- Protect the property from further damage and make reasonable and necessary repairs to protect it.
- Prepare an inventory of damaged personal property showing the quantity, description, actual cash value and amount of loss, with bills, receipts and related documents.

**How the proof of loss affects payment:** Under the homeowners policy, loss will be payable 60 days after we receive your proof of loss and an agreement is reached, a final judgment is entered, or an appraisal award is filed with us. Payment timing depends on one of those three things happening as well, not only on our receiving your proof of loss.

**If this is an auto claim:** The Personal Auto Policy sections I have don't set a deadline for a proof of loss. They do require that we must be notified promptly of how, when and where the accident or loss happened and that you promptly send us copies of any notices or legal papers received in connection with the accident or loss. If you have an auto claim, please confirm the deadline with your adjuster.

rows.question: Will you pay replacement cost or actual cash value for my roof repair?
rows.answer:
**Your roof is settled at replacement cost, with no deduction for depreciation, but only if you carry enough insurance on your home and only after the repair is actually done.** Until then, you'd receive actual cash value. This assumes the damage is covered and the roof is part of a building insured under Coverage A (your home) or Coverage B (other structures). I can't confirm either of those without knowing the cause of damage and your policy details.

**The basic rule**

Buildings under Coverage A or B are settled at replacement cost without deduction for depreciation. "Replacement cost" means the cost to repair or replace damaged property with material of like kind and quality, for the same use, without deduction for depreciation.

**Condition 1: You need enough insurance (the 80% rule)**

- If at the time of loss, the amount of insurance on the damaged building is 80% or more of its full replacement cost, we will pay the cost to repair or replace, up to the limit of liability.
- If your coverage is less than 80% of what it would cost to rebuild your home, we will pay the greater of the actual cash value of the damaged part or that proportion of the cost to repair or replace that the limit of insurance bears to 80% of the replacement cost. In plain terms, being underinsured can reduce your payment.

Which of these applies depends on the coverage amount on your Declarations page compared with your home's full replacement cost.

**Condition 2: Full replacement cost comes after the repair is done**

- We will pay no more than actual cash value until actual repair or replacement is complete.
- Actual cash value means the cost to repair or replace damaged property with property of like kind and quality, less a deduction for depreciation, including physical deterioration and obsolescence. For a roof, that usually means an older roof is worth less at first.
- You may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss. Keep that 180-day deadline in mind if you plan to collect the rest after repairs.

This explains what your policy language says. It isn't a coverage decision or a promise of payment. Your adjuster will determine whether the damage is covered and the final amount.

rows.question: I disagree with the adjuster's estimate. What can I do?
rows.answer:
**If this is a homeowners (HO-3) claim, you can demand an appraisal.** Under the policy, if you and we fail to agree on the amount of loss, either may demand an appraisal of the loss.

**How appraisal works:**
- **Each side picks an appraiser.** Each party will choose a competent and impartial appraiser within 20 days after receiving a written request from the other.
- **The appraisers pick a tie-breaker.** The two appraisers will choose an umpire.
- **Two out of three decides.** A decision agreed to by any two will set the amount of loss.
- **Costs are split.** Each party pays its own appraiser and shares equally the expense of the umpire. You should weigh this cost against how far apart you and the adjuster are.

**When payment happens:** Under the policy, loss will be payable 60 days after we receive your proof of loss and an agreement is reached, a final judgment is entered, or an appraisal award is filed with us.

**Things to check first:**
- **Is the gap about how your belongings are valued?** Personal property, awnings, carpeting, household appliances and outdoor antennas are settled at actual cash value at the time of loss but not more than the amount required to repair or replace, unless a Personal Property Replacement Cost endorsement is shown in the Declarations. If the adjuster subtracted for age and wear, that may be why. Look at your Declarations page to see if you have that endorsement.
- **Is the deductible the reason?** The policy pays only that part of the total of all loss payable that exceeds the deductible amount shown in the Declarations. A separate windstorm or hail deductible may apply if shown by endorsement.
- **Have you documented the loss?** Your duties include preparing an inventory of damaged personal property showing the quantity, description, actual cash value and amount of loss, with bills, receipts and related documents, and sending us within 60 days after our request, your signed, sworn proof of loss. Good receipts and records can help you make your case, whether you negotiate with the adjuster or go to appraisal.

**If this is an auto claim:** The auto policy sections I have do not include an appraisal process. They say our limit of liability for loss will be the lesser of the actual cash value of the stolen or damaged property, or the amount necessary to repair or replace the property with other property of like kind and quality, and that an adjustment for depreciation and physical condition will be made in determining actual cash value in the event of a total loss. Please tell me which policy your claim is under so I can point you to the right language.

This explains what the policy says. It is not a decision on your claim or a promise of any payment amount.

rows.question: How long do I have to sue the insurance company?
rows.answer:
**Under the homeowners policy (HO-3), you have two years from the date of loss to file a lawsuit against us, and only if you've first fully complied with the policy's terms.** The policy says no action can be brought against us unless there has been full compliance with all of the terms under this Section and the action is started within two years after the date of loss.

In plain terms, two conditions must both be met:
1. **Timing:** The lawsuit must be started within two years after the date the loss happened, not the date you filed your claim or got a decision.
2. **Compliance:** You must have met your obligations under the policy's conditions before suing.

**If your question is about an auto policy:** The Personal Auto Policy sections available to me don't include a deadline for suing. They do say we have no duty to provide coverage under this policy unless there has been full compliance with the following duties. These duties include notifying us promptly about the accident or loss and cooperating with the investigation. If you need the auto deadline, please ask about that specifically or check the full policy.

This explains the base homeowners form. Your state wasn't specified, so I haven't been able to check whether a state endorsement changes this deadline. If you tell me where the property is located, I can check whether an endorsement applies.

rows.question: How long do I have to sue the insurance company?
rows.answer:
**For a California homeowners policy, you generally have two years from the date of loss to file a lawsuit, but California pauses that clock while your claim is being reviewed.**

**The basic rule (HO-3 policy):** No action can be brought against us unless there has been full compliance with all of the terms under this Section and the action is started within two years after the date of loss. This means you must also have met the policy's requirements before you can sue.

**California change:** Because your property is in California, the California endorsement changes this rule and controls. The two-year period to bring an action is tolled from the time you give notice of the claim until we formally deny the claim in writing. In plain terms, the two-year clock stops from the day you report the claim and doesn't start again until the company denies the claim in writing. You may therefore have more than two calendar years from the date of loss, depending on how long the claim was open.

**Things to keep in mind:**
- The pause starts only once you give notice of the claim, so reporting promptly matters.
- These rules come from the homeowners policy. The auto policy sections provided don't include a time limit for lawsuits, so if your question is about an auto claim, I can't answer it from these documents.
- This explains the policy wording. It isn't legal advice about your deadline. For a specific dispute, consider talking with an attorney to confirm the exact date that applies to you.

rows.question: A guest slipped on my stairs. Will you pay their medical bills?
rows.answer:
**Your homeowners policy may cover your guest's medical bills under Coverage F (Medical Payments to Others), depending on a few conditions.** I can't confirm payment, but here's what the policy says.

**What's covered**
The policy says we will pay the necessary medical expenses that are incurred or medically ascertained within three years from the date of an accident causing bodily injury, to a person on the insured location with the permission of an insured.

**Conditions that apply to your situation**
- **Where it happened:** The guest must have been hurt on the insured location, meaning the property covered by your policy. If your stairs are at your insured home, this condition would be met.
- **Permission:** The guest must have been there with permission from you or another insured.
- **Who's covered:** This coverage does not apply to you or regular residents of your household. A visiting guest qualifies. A person who lives with you does not.
- **Time limit:** Only necessary medical expenses incurred or medically ascertained within three years from the date of the fall are covered.

**How much is covered**
The limit is shown in the Declarations and is typically $1,000 or $5,000 per person. Check your Declarations page to see your exact limit.

**What this depends on**
This assumes you have the HO-3 homeowners policy with Coverage F. Whether the bills are paid will depend on the facts above and on the limit shown on your Declarations page. A claims adjuster will make the final decision, so report the incident to us or your agent.

rows.question: Am I covered if I crash while driving for Uber?
rows.answer:
**Generally no. Your policy provides no coverage while you're logged on to Uber, unless your Declarations page shows a Ride-Share and Delivery endorsement.** The policy states it does not provide any coverage while your covered auto is being used to transport passengers or deliver goods for compensation through a transportation network company or delivery platform, from the time the driver logs on to the platform until the time the driver logs off, unless a Ride-Share and Delivery endorsement is shown in the Declarations.

**What this depends on:**

- **Whether you have the Ride-Share and Delivery endorsement.** Check your Declarations page. If the endorsement is listed, the exclusion above doesn't apply. I don't have that endorsement's terms, so I can't tell you what it covers or what its limits are.
- **Whether you were logged on to the app.** The exclusion runs from the time you log on until the time you log off, so it applies even between rides while you're logged on.

**Other parts of the policy that may also limit coverage:**

- **Damage to your car:** The policy won't pay for loss to your covered auto which occurs while it is being used as a public or livery conveyance.
- **Medical payments:** There's no Medical Payments Coverage for injuries while occupying your covered auto when it is being used as a public or livery conveyance.

This explains what the policy language says and isn't a final coverage decision. For your specific situation, check your Declarations page and contact your agent or Cobalt Harbor Mutual claims.

rows.question: My car was stolen. Will you pay for a rental car?
rows.answer:
**Yes, the policy provides some help with temporary transportation, such as a rental car, after your car is stolen, but there is a daily and total cap and a waiting period.** This is what the policy language says, not a final decision on your claim.

**What the policy pays**
- The policy will pay up to $20 per day, to a maximum of $600, for temporary transportation expenses incurred by you because of the total theft of your covered auto. This applies only when the whole car is stolen, not parts or items from it.
- This is paid in addition to our limit of liability [Applies only when your car has been stolen.] and without application of a deductible [Applies only when your car has been stolen.].

**When the coverage starts and stops**
- The policy covers only expenses incurred during the period beginning 48 hours after the theft and ending when your covered auto is returned or we pay for its loss. Rental costs from the first two days after the theft aren't covered under this provision.

**If you bought Rental Reimbursement coverage**
- If a Rental Reimbursement endorsement is shown in the Declarations, its daily and maximum limits apply instead. [Applies only when your car has been stolen.] Check your Declarations page to see whether you have this endorsement and what its limits are. Those limits would replace the $20/day and $600 figures above.

**What you should do now**
- The policy requires you to promptly notify the police if your covered auto or any non-owned auto is stolen. If you haven't filed a police report yet, do so as soon as possible.

rows.question: I hit a deer. Is that collision or comprehensive?
rows.answer:
**Hitting a deer counts as comprehensive, not collision.** Your policy lists contact with bird or animal among the causes of loss that are considered other than collision (comprehensive).

**Whether this is covered depends on your Declarations page:**
- The policy pays for comprehensive damage to your car only if the Declarations indicate that Other Than Collision Coverage is provided. Check your Declarations page to confirm you have this coverage.
- If you do, payment is for direct and accidental loss to your covered auto or any non-owned auto, including their equipment, minus any applicable deductible shown in the Declarations. Your comprehensive deductible is listed there.

For comparison, "collision" means the upset of your covered auto or a non-owned auto or their impact with another vehicle or object. Because animal contact is specifically listed as comprehensive, a deer strike falls under comprehensive.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a final coverage decision. Your claim will be reviewed based on the facts of the loss and your actual coverages.

rows.question: I just bought a second car. How long do I have to add it to my policy?
rows.answer:
**You have 14 days from the date you become the owner to ask us to add your second car.** Under the Personal Auto Policy (§1.2), if it is an additional vehicle, coverage begins on the date you become the owner, but you must ask us to insure it within 14 days after you become the owner.

What this means for you:
- **Start counting from the purchase date.** The 14 days begin when you became the owner, not when you first drive the car or register it.
- **Coverage starts on the ownership date, but only if you meet the deadline.** The car has coverage from the day you became the owner, as long as you ask us to insure it within those 14 days.
- **The rule only applies to cars bought during the policy period.** The policy defines this situation as a car you become the owner of during the policy period.

**If the new car replaces a car on your policy instead of being an extra one, a different rule applies.** If it replaces a vehicle shown in the Declarations, it has the same coverage as the vehicle it replaced, and you must ask us to insure it within 14 days only if you wish to add or continue Physical Damage coverage.

The details of your coverage, such as which coverages and limits apply to the new car, depend on your policy and Declarations page. To be safe, contact us to add the car as soon as you can, well within the 14 days.

rows.question: Someone hit my car and drove off. What do I need to do?
rows.answer:
**Report the hit-and-run to the police within 24 hours, and report it to us within 30 days.** Your policy says that a hit-and-run accident must be reported to police within 24 hours and to us within 30 days.

**How your policy treats a hit-and-run**

Uninsured Motorist coverage can apply to a hit-and-run driver. The policy defines an uninsured vehicle to include one which is a hit-and-run vehicle whose operator or owner cannot be identified and which hits you, a family member, or a vehicle you or a family member are occupying. In plain terms, this part of the policy applies only if the driver can't be identified and the vehicle hit you, a family member, or a car one of you was in at the time.

This coverage is for injuries. The policy says we will pay compensatory damages which an insured is legally entitled to recover from the owner or operator of an uninsured motor vehicle because of bodily injury sustained by an insured and caused by an accident.

**What I can't tell from the policy sections I have**

- **Whether you were in the car.** If your car was parked and empty, it may not fit the hit-and-run definition above. That definition requires the vehicle to hit you, a family member, or a car one of you was occupying.
- **Damage to your car.** The sections available to me describe injury coverage only. Whether repairs to your car are covered depends on what other coverages you have, such as collision. Those coverages would be listed on your Declarations page, and I don't have that information.

**Practical next steps**

1. Call the police right away if you haven't already. You must report within 24 hours.
2. Contact Cobalt Harbor Mutual to report the claim. You must report within 30 days, but sooner is better.
3. Tell us whether anyone was hurt and whether you or a family member were in the car.

I'm explaining what the policy language says. The final coverage decision will be made by the claims team after they review your claim.

rows.question: Does my auto policy cover me in Mexico?
rows.answer:
**Based on the policy language, no. Mexico is not included in the area where your auto policy applies.**

The Policy Territory section says this policy applies only to accidents and losses which occur within the United States of America, its territories or possessions, Puerto Rico, or Canada, or while your covered auto is being transported between their ports. Mexico isn't on that list, so an accident or loss that happens while you're driving in Mexico would fall outside the policy territory.

The documents I have don't include any endorsement or option that extends coverage to Mexico. If you plan to drive there, contact your agent or Cobalt Harbor Mutual before your trip to ask about your options.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a final coverage decision.

rows.question: What's my reserve authority as an associate adjuster?
rows.answer:
As an Associate Adjuster (Level 1), your standard reserve authority is **$25,000 per claim**. During a declared catastrophe, it is temporarily raised for certain claims.

**Standard authority (CHG §2.1)**
- Adjusters may set and change reserves only within their authority level, and Level 1 (Associate Adjuster): up to $25,000 per claim.
- If a reserve needs to go higher, it requires the next authority level: Level 2 (Senior Adjuster): up to $100,000 per claim, Level 3 (Claims Supervisor): up to $250,000 per claim, and above $250,000: Regional Claims Manager approval is required.

**Catastrophe exception (CHG §2.3)**
- During a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud. The $50,000 limit applies only when all three conditions are met: there is a declared catastrophe, the claim is a windstorm or hail claim, and there is no suspected fraud. Otherwise, your $25,000 limit still applies.

**Related reserve requirements (CHG §2.2)**
- Reserves must be reviewed every 30 days and whenever material new information is received. A reserve change of more than 50% in a single adjustment requires a file note explaining the reason.

rows.question: What's my reserve authority as an associate adjuster on a hail claim during a catastrophe?
rows.answer:
**During a declared catastrophe, your Level 1 reserve authority on a hail claim is $50,000, unless the claim involves suspected fraud.** If fraud is suspected, the standard $25,000 Level 1 limit applies.

**Supporting detail:**

- **Standard authority (CHG §2.1):** Adjusters may set and change reserves only within their authority level, and Level 1 (Associate Adjuster): up to $25,000 per claim.
- **Catastrophe increase (CHG §2.3):** During a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud. The increase is temporary and requires all of the following:
  - The catastrophe is declared.
  - The claim is windstorm or hail.
  - There is no suspected fraud.
- **Above your authority:** If the reserve needs to exceed your applicable limit, it goes to the next level. Level 2 (Senior Adjuster): up to $100,000 per claim. Level 3 (Claims Supervisor): up to $250,000 per claim.

**Related reserve requirements (CHG §2.2):** Reserves must be reviewed every 30 days and whenever material new information is received. A reserve change of more than 50% in a single adjustment requires a file note explaining the reason.

rows.question: When do I need to refer a claim to SIU?
rows.answer:
Refer a claim to SIU **within 5 business days** when **two or more** fraud indicators are present (CHG §3.1). Refer the claim to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) within 5 business days if two or more of the following indicators are present:

- The policy was purchased or coverage increased within 60 days before the loss.
- The insured is unusually familiar with claims procedures or insurance terminology.
- The insured pressures for a quick settlement or offers to accept a lower amount in cash.
- Receipts or documents appear altered, or the insured cannot produce proof of ownership for high-value items.
- The loss occurs shortly after the insured disclosed financial difficulty.
- Multiple prior claims of a similar type within 36 months.

A single indicator on its own does not trigger the referral requirement under §3.1. The threshold is two or more.

**After referral (CHG §3.2):** While a claim is under SIU review, continue to handle the claim in good faith and meet all regulatory deadlines. Do not disclose the SIU referral to the insured.

**Related, catastrophe authority (CHG §2.3):** If you're working a declared catastrophe, note that during a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud. So the raised authority does not apply to a windstorm or hail claim where fraud is suspected.

rows.question: How fast do I need to contact the insured on a bodily injury claim?
rows.answer:
On any claim involving bodily injury, you must make first contact with the insured within 4 business hours of FNOL.

Per CHG §1.1, the assigned adjuster must make first contact with the insured within 24 hours of first notice of loss (FNOL) for property claims and within 4 business hours for any claim involving bodily injury. If a claim involves both property damage and bodily injury, the 4-business-hour standard applies because the guideline covers "any claim involving bodily injury."

Also, document the contact attempt in the claim file even if unsuccessful.

rows.question: Is a 22-year-old roof eligible for replacement cost on new business?
rows.answer:
**Not automatically.** Under UWG §1.1, new business is eligible for replacement cost on roof surfacing only if the roof is 20 years old or less. A 22-year-old roof is over that threshold.

**What §1.1 requires for this risk:** Roofs older than 20 years require an actual cash value roof endorsement or an inspection showing at least 5 years of remaining life. You have two options:

- **ACV roof endorsement:** Attach the endorsement so the roof surfacing is settled on an actual cash value basis.
- **Inspection:** Obtain an inspection. It satisfies §1.1 only if it shows at least 5 years of remaining roof life.

§1.1 doesn't say what happens if the inspection shows less than 5 years of remaining life. The ACV roof endorsement is the alternative route the guideline provides.

**Other new-business requirements:** Under UWG §2.1, every new business and every third renewal requires a replacement cost estimate using the approved estimator. Coverage A must be at least 100% of the estimated replacement cost at new business.

rows.question: When do I refer a risk to a senior underwriter?
rows.answer:
Under UWG §3.1, refer a risk to a senior underwriter if it meets any one of three thresholds: Coverage A above $1,500,000, any dwelling built before 1940, or any wildfire risk score of 8 or higher on the 10-point scale.

**Referral triggers (any one is enough):**
- Coverage A above $1,500,000
- Dwelling built before 1940
- Wildfire risk score of 8 or higher on the 10-point scale

**Additional approval for the highest wildfire scores:** A senior underwriter referral alone is not enough for scores of 9 or 10. Underwriters may not bind wildfire risk scores of 9 or 10 without Regional Underwriting Manager approval. A score of 8 triggers referral, while 9 or 10 also requires RUM sign-off before binding.

**Check eligibility first:** Referral thresholds apply to otherwise eligible risks. UWG §1.3 lists risks that are ineligible altogether: dwellings in foreclosure; dwellings vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 days; properties with an unfenced swimming pool; properties used for short-term rental more than 30 days per year without a home-sharing endorsement; and dwellings with knob-and-tube wiring.

These guidelines are from CHM-UWG 2026.1 and apply in all jurisdictions.

unsupported_claims: "Referral thresholds apply to otherwise eligible risks" (and the instruction to check eligibility first): neither UWG §3.1 nor §1.3 states that referral thresholds apply only to eligible risks or that eligibility must be checked before referral.

rows.question: Can we write a house with a swimming pool?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether the pool is fenced.** Under UWG §1.3, properties with an unfenced swimming pool are listed as ineligible. A pool alone does not make the risk ineligible under this section; the lack of fencing does.

**What this means for the submission:**
- **Unfenced pool:** Ineligible under §1.3.
- **Fenced pool:** §1.3 does not list it as ineligible. However, this section only lists ineligible risks. Other guidelines, such as rating, liability limits, or pool-specific requirements, may still apply but don't appear in the material provided. Confirm against the full guidelines before binding.

**Other §1.3 ineligibility criteria to check on the same risk:** dwellings in foreclosure; dwellings vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 days; properties used for short-term rental more than 30 days per year without a home-sharing endorsement; and dwellings with knob-and-tube wiring.

The guideline doesn't define what counts as adequate fencing, such as height, gates, or full enclosure. If the fencing is partial or questionable, verify the standard before treating the pool as fenced.

rows.question: If my house burns down, do I have to list every item I lost to get paid for my belongings?
rows.answer:
**Generally yes, but there's a California exception.** If your home is a total loss **and the loss relates to a declared state of emergency** (for example, a wildfire that triggers an official emergency declaration), the California endorsement requires us to offer you a partial payment for your belongings without an itemized list. Otherwise, the standard policy asks for an inventory.

**The standard rule (base HO-3 policy)**
After a loss, one of your duties is to prepare an inventory of damaged personal property showing the quantity, description, actual cash value and amount of loss, with bills, receipts and related documents.

**The California exception for declared emergencies**
Because you're in California, the state endorsement adds this: in the event of a covered total loss of the dwelling relating to a declared state of emergency, we will offer a payment under Coverage C of no less than 30% of the Coverage C limit, up to $250,000, without requiring an itemized inventory. (Coverage C is the part of your policy that covers your personal belongings.)

What this means:
- It applies only if the home is a **total loss**, the loss is **covered**, and it **relates to a declared state of emergency**. A house fire that isn't tied to a declared emergency wouldn't qualify.
- The no-inventory payment is **at least 30% of your Coverage C limit, capped at $250,000**. Your Coverage C limit is shown on your Declarations page.
- These sources describe this as an advance and don't say how the rest of a belongings claim is handled. Beyond that amount, you should expect the standard inventory requirement to apply.

**Is fire covered for belongings?**
Yes. Fire is one of the named perils for personal property: We insure Coverage C personal property for direct physical loss caused only by the following named perils: fire or lightning; ...

**Another California benefit for declared emergencies**
For a total loss relating to a declared state of emergency, the 180-day period in HO-3 Section 6.3 to make a claim for additional replacement cost is replaced with a period of no less than 36 months from the date of the first actual cash value payment. So in that situation, you have much longer to claim the full replacement cost after your first payment.

Whether these benefits apply depends on the facts of your loss, especially whether there was a declared state of emergency. Your adjuster makes the final coverage decision. If you have a loss, give prompt notice to us or our agent.

unsupported_claims: Your Coverage C limit is shown on your Declarations page.
Beyond that amount, you should expect the standard inventory requirement to apply (the sources do not say how the remainder of a belongings claim is handled after the advance).

rows.question: After a total loss, how long do I have to collect the rest of the replacement cost?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether your total loss relates to a declared state of emergency.** If it does, California gives you at least 36 months from your first actual cash value payment. If it doesn't, the standard policy gives you 180 days after the loss.

**How replacement cost is paid**
Your policy pays in two steps. The policy states that we will pay no more than actual cash value until actual repair or replacement is complete. You may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost. The "rest" of the replacement cost is that second claim. Actual cash value is the depreciated value. Replacement cost is the full cost to rebuild without subtracting for depreciation.

**Your deadline**
- **If the total loss relates to a declared state of emergency (for example, a declared wildfire disaster):** The California endorsement replaces the standard deadline. For a total loss relating to a declared state of emergency, the 180-day period in HO-3 Section 6.3 to make a claim for additional replacement cost is replaced with a period of no less than 36 months from the date of the first actual cash value payment. This clock starts when you receive your first actual cash value payment, not on the date of the loss.
- **If the total loss does not relate to a declared state of emergency:** The standard policy deadline applies. You must claim the additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss.

**Related points**
- **Rebuilding elsewhere:** Under the California endorsement, if you choose to rebuild or replace the dwelling at a location other than the residence premises, we will pay the replacement cost of the dwelling, up to the Coverage A limit, measured as the cost to rebuild at the original residence premises. The value of the land at the new location is not included.
- **Your amount of insurance matters:** Full replacement cost depends on carrying enough coverage. If your coverage is less than 80% of the home's full replacement cost, the payment can be reduced.
- **Belongings advance:** The California endorsement offers a contents advance only for a covered total loss of the dwelling relating to a declared state of emergency. In that case, we will offer a payment under Coverage C of no less than 30% of the Coverage C limit, up to $250,000, without requiring an itemized inventory.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a coverage decision. Your adjuster can confirm which deadline applies to your claim.

rows.question: Is mold from a slow leak covered?
rows.answer:
**It depends on how long the leak went on.** Mold is covered only when it comes from a covered cause of loss, and a leak lasting 14 or more days is not a covered cause. So mold from a long-running slow leak may not be covered, while mold from a shorter leak may be covered up to $10,000.

**Mold coverage and its limit**
Your policy will pay up to $10,000 in total for direct physical loss caused by fungi, mold, wet or dry rot, or bacteria, including the cost to remove it and to tear out and replace covered property to gain access, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst. The $10,000 is the most we will pay regardless of the number of locations or claims during the policy period.

**Why the length of the leak matters**
Among the causes of loss the policy does not cover is continuous or repeated seepage or leakage of water or steam over a period of 14 or more days from within a plumbing, heating or air conditioning system or household appliance. This means:
- **Leak of 14 or more days:** The leak is not a covered peril, so the $10,000 mold coverage, which applies only when mold results from a covered peril, would likely not apply.
- **Leak shorter than 14 days:** If the leak is otherwise a covered peril, the mold coverage may apply, up to $10,000 in total and only when the mold results from that covered peril.

**What isn't covered either way**
Where the policy covers water damage resulting from a plumbing system or appliance problem, it pays to tear out and replace part of the building to reach the system, but not the system or appliance itself. In other words, it does not pay to fix the leaking pipe or appliance.

**What a decision will depend on**
- How long the leak was happening, and whether it started suddenly
- Where the water came from

An adjuster will look at these facts. This explanation is not a coverage decision. If you think you have a claim, report it and describe when you first noticed the leak and the mold.

rows.question: My pipes froze while I was away for the winter. Is that covered?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether you took reasonable steps to protect your pipes before you left.** Your policy excludes freezing of a plumbing system while the dwelling is vacant or unoccupied, unless you used reasonable care to maintain heat or shut off the water supply and drain the system. I can't make the final coverage decision, but here's how the policy language works.

**The key question: what did you do before leaving?**
- If you kept the heat on, or shut off the water and drained the pipes, the freezing exclusion doesn't apply.
- If you did neither, the freezing exclusion likely applies because the home was unoccupied while you were away.

**Water damage to your home**
If the frozen pipes burst and caused water damage, the policy says that if any of these cause water damage not otherwise excluded, we cover the resulting water damage, including the cost of tearing out and replacing part of the building to access the system, but not the system or appliance itself. This means:
- The resulting water damage, including opening walls or floors to reach the pipes, may be covered, but only if that water damage isn't otherwise excluded.
- The cost to repair or replace the frozen pipes themselves is not covered.

**Your belongings (furniture, clothing, etc.)**
Personal property is covered only for specific listed causes. That list includes both accidental discharge or overflow of water or steam and freezing.

**Mold, if it develops**
The policy pays up to $10,000 in total for direct physical loss caused by fungi, mold, wet or dry rot, or bacteria, including the cost to remove it and to tear out and replace covered property to gain access, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst. So mold coverage applies only if the water damage itself came from a covered cause.

**A slow leak is treated differently**
If the pipe leaked slowly rather than bursting suddenly, note that the policy excludes continuous or repeated seepage or leakage of water or steam over a period of 14 or more days from within a plumbing, heating or air conditioning system or household appliance. Since you were away for the winter, how long the water was leaking may matter.

**Next steps:** When you report the claim, be ready to explain how you left the home. For example, say what temperature the thermostat was set to, or whether the water was shut off and the pipes drained. Also say roughly when the damage likely happened. Your adjuster will use these details to decide coverage.

rows.question: Will hail damage to my roof be paid at replacement cost?
rows.answer:
**It depends on how old your roof surfacing is and what kind of damage the hail caused.** If your policy includes the Texas Windstorm and Hail Deductible Endorsement, that endorsement changes the standard HO-3 rules for hail damage to your roof. Where they differ, the Texas endorsement controls.

**1. Roof age determines replacement cost or actual cash value**
- **More than 15 years old:** Hail damage to roof surfacing is settled at actual cash value, not replacement cost, if the roof surfacing is more than 15 years old at the time of loss. Actual cash value generally means depreciation is taken into account.
- **15 years old or less:** Roof surfacing 15 years old or less is settled under HO-3 Section 6.3, the standard replacement cost rules.

**2. Replacement cost for a roof 15 years old or less has conditions**
- **Full replacement cost requires insuring at least 80%.** If, at the time of loss, the amount of insurance on the damaged building is 80% or more of its full replacement cost, we will pay the cost to repair or replace, up to the limit of liability.
- **Below 80%, the payment is reduced.** If it is less than 80%, we will pay the greater of the actual cash value of the damaged part or that proportion of the cost to repair or replace that the limit of insurance bears to 80% of the replacement cost. Your Declarations page shows your coverage amount, which you can compare to your home's full replacement cost.
- **The full amount comes after repairs are done.** We will pay no more than actual cash value until actual repair or replacement is complete. You may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss.

**3. Cosmetic hail damage isn't covered at all**
Regardless of roof age, we do not cover cosmetic damage to roof surfacing caused by hail. Cosmetic damage means marring, pitting or denting that changes the appearance of the roof surface but does not prevent the roof from continuing to function as a barrier to water entering the dwelling, and does not shorten the expected life of the roof. Dents that only affect appearance would not be paid.

**A related tip:** If hail has damaged your roof and you need to protect it from further damage, the policy says we will pay the reasonable cost incurred by you for necessary measures taken solely to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage, such as tarping a damaged roof or boarding broken windows. Keep receipts for these expenses.

This explains what the policy language says. The final outcome of your claim depends on your roof's age, the type of damage, and your coverage amounts, which an adjuster will review.

rows.question: Will you pay for a rental car while my car is in the shop after a crash?
rows.answer:
**Based on the policy sections I have, the built-in rental benefit doesn't cover a car that's in the shop after a crash. It applies only when your car is stolen.**

**What the policy says**

The Personal Auto Policy pays for temporary transportation, like a rental car, only for a stolen vehicle. In addition to our limit of liability, we will pay, without application of a deductible, up to $20 per day, to a maximum of $600, for temporary transportation expenses incurred by you because of the total theft of your covered auto. The timing is also limited to theft situations. We will pay only expenses incurred during the period beginning 48 hours after the theft and ending when your covered auto is returned or we pay for its loss.

**Whether you have extra rental coverage**

The policy refers to an optional Rental Reimbursement endorsement. It says if a Rental Reimbursement endorsement is shown in the Declarations, its daily and maximum limits apply instead. The sections I have only describe that endorsement replacing the limits for theft. They don't say whether it covers a rental while your car is being repaired after a crash.

**Next steps**

- Check your **Declarations page**, the summary page of your policy, to see whether a Rental Reimbursement endorsement is listed.
- If it is, ask your agent or claims representative whether it covers rentals during collision repairs and what its daily and maximum limits are.

This explains the policy wording only. It is not a final coverage decision.

rows.question: Will you pay for building code upgrades when I rebuild?
rows.answer:
**Not under the standard homeowners policy by itself. Code upgrades are covered only if your policy includes an Ordinance or Law endorsement listed on your Declarations page.**

The HO-3 policy says: "We do not cover the increased cost of construction required by any ordinance or law regulating the construction, repair or demolition of a building, except as provided by an Ordinance or Law endorsement if shown in the Declarations."

**What this means for you:**

rows.question: Can an associate adjuster set a $40,000 reserve on a hail claim?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether a catastrophe has been declared and whether fraud is suspected.** Under standard authority, a $40,000 reserve is above Level 1 limits. However, during a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud.

**Standard authority (CHG §2.1)**
- Adjusters may set and change reserves only within their authority level.
- Level 1 (Associate Adjuster): up to $25,000 per claim.
- Level 2 (Senior Adjuster): up to $100,000 per claim.

**Outcomes for this claim**
- **Declared catastrophe and no suspected fraud:** The associate adjuster can set the $40,000 reserve. The CAT exception raises Level 1 authority to $50,000 for hail claims, and $40,000 is within that limit.
- **No declared catastrophe, or fraud is suspected:** The $25,000 Level 1 limit applies. The $40,000 reserve would need a Level 2 Senior Adjuster or higher.

**Related reserve requirement (CHG §2.2)**
If this is a change to an existing reserve, keep in mind that a reserve change of more than 50% in a single adjustment requires a file note explaining the reason. Also, reserves must be reviewed every 30 days and whenever material new information is received.

rows.question: My detached garage burned down. Is it covered and up to what amount?
rows.answer:
**Your detached garage falls under Coverage B (Other Structures), and its limit is 10% of your dwelling (Coverage A) limit unless your Declarations page shows a different amount.** I can't confirm a final dollar figure or guarantee payment, because that depends on the limits on your Declarations page and the details of your claim.

**What's covered**
- Coverage B applies to other structures on the residence premises set apart from the dwelling by clear space, such as a detached garage, fence or shed.
- The limit for Coverage B is 10% of the Coverage A limit unless a different limit is shown in the Declarations. For example, if your dwelling limit were $300,000 and your Declarations don't show a different Coverage B limit, the garage limit would be $30,000.
- **One exception:** We do not cover other structures rented to any person who is not a tenant of the dwelling, unless used solely as a private garage. If you rented the garage to someone outside your household, this could matter.

**Fire as the cause**
- The excerpts I have don't include the list of perils that applies to structures under Coverage B, so I can't quote that language directly.
- Fire is listed as a covered peril for your personal belongings. We insure Coverage C personal property for direct physical loss caused only by the following named perils: fire or lightning, among others. This means items stored in the garage may also be covered under Coverage C.
- Even if an earthquake or other earth movement started the fire, the policy says we do cover direct loss by fire or explosion that results from earth movement.

**Debris removal**
- We will pay your reasonable expense for the removal of debris of covered property if a covered peril causes the loss. This expense is included in the limit of liability that applies to the damaged property.
- If the amount to be paid for the actual damage plus debris removal exceeds the limit, an additional 5% of that limit is available for debris removal.

**Your deductible**
- We will pay only that part of the total of all loss payable that exceeds the deductible amount shown in the Declarations.

**Next step:** Check your Declarations page for your Coverage A limit, any separate Coverage B limit, and your deductible. Then contact your adjuster to start the claim.

rows.question: Sewage came up through my basement drain. Covered?
rows.answer:
**Under the standard HO-3 policy, sewage backing up through a drain is not covered. You may have coverage if you added a water backup endorsement to your policy.**

**What the standard policy says:** The water exclusions state that the policy does not cover loss caused by water or water-borne material that backs up through sewers or drains or overflows from a sump pump.

**The exception:** Water backup coverage is available by endorsement with a sublimit. A sublimit means this coverage has its own, usually lower, maximum dollar amount. The search results don't say what that amount is. Whether you have this coverage depends on whether the endorsement was added to your policy. To check:
- Look at your Declarations page, the summary page of your policy, for a water backup endorsement and its limit.
- If you're unsure, contact your agent or Cobalt Harbor Mutual.

**If the cause was flooding:** If water from outside, such as a flood or surface water, caused the backup, a separate exclusion applies. The policy does not cover flood, surface water, waves, tidal water, or overflow of a body of water, whether or not driven by wind, and flood coverage is available only through a separate flood policy.
